note: Your way through (book/scripts/modules/way-through.mjs): why each chapter is in the book, what it holds for the chapters after it, one wonder a single edit past a room's own line, and the pairings a reader may keep apart. Held by book:check; written out as canon by npm run spw:way. A swap adds no spoken line.

1.reason: A wish has to be something you can hold and cannot file, so the first chapter makes it warm and has the maps refuse it. The reader learns early that being recorded and being real are different jobs.
1.holds: Boof dug a warm egg out of a frozen furrow. It was an unspent wish, and no map in Boon.land would take it down.

wonder.says: The same warm ground, read by the ones who live under it.
wonder.asks: Who is the furrow warm for?

2.reason: Before anyone can want the egg, the land has to practise wanting. The grove repeats things a beat late so a reader gets used to futures that sound like memories.
2.holds: The grove answered the egg a beat late, rehearsing futures it had not decided to grant.

wonder.says: An echo that acts where it used to repeat.
wonder.asks: If the echo chose, what would it choose?
ways: Still a beat too late to matter

3.reason: Wish stories usually take the genie for granted. This one opens his practice in the sand, so the reader meets a professional who can price anything and cannot see a small want.
3.holds: Boof's weight settled two old roads into one turn, and she dug up a retired Genie who could grant anything and could not read what she wanted.

wonder.says: The same turn, seen by someone who used to sell them.
wonder.asks: What does he make of a road settled with no miracle asked?
ways: He knows he is out of work

4.reason: The book needs a fair hearing for the worst idea in it. Mr. BaneWAP gets a council and a good argument, because a villain nobody could agree with would teach nothing.
4.holds: The council had no law for the egg. Mr. BaneWAP argued it should be filed and auctioned to himself, and every key on the hill failed to fit it.

wonder.says: The mirror that shows what wanting becomes, read by the one who wants the most.
wonder.asks: What does the mirror show Mr. BaneWAP?
ways: His own crust, from the outside
Something sweet he does not recognise

5.reason: Two claims need somewhere to be equally wrong. The floor parts so the argument has a physics, and the Genie can say the rule the rest of the book stands on: a small turn costs a little, a grand one is still being paid.
5.holds: Two claims pulled at the egg until the floor parted. The Genie taught what wishing costs: a small turn costs a little, and a grand one is still being paid.

wonder.says: Measure becomes action: he mends it before he has finished listening.
wonder.asks: What happens if the crack is mended first?

6.reason: Up to here everything given has cost something. Mr. BoonWAP is the counter-example, delightful and slightly alarming, so a reader can enjoy abundance before asking what it would take to be him.
6.holds: In Bonk City, Mr. BoonWAP fed a plaza from himself and was no smaller, and asked Boof the one question she could not answer yet. She kept a slice, warm in waxed paper.

wonder.says: He stops asking and answers it for her.
wonder.asks: If he answered his own question, what would her wish become?

7.reason: A promise is the first thing Boof does on purpose. The oath is cheap to swear and costly to keep, and the shadow clause says aloud that someone else usually pays.
7.holds: At the market stone Boof swore to spend the wish only when the want is true, and learned that every spent wish owes a coincidence to a stranger.

wonder.says: The same oath, read from where its shadow lands.
ways: They are someone you have met

8.reason: The Genie's trade needs a day at work. Pricing a tavern's wishes shows that ordinary wants resist his machinery more than empires do, which is what makes hers impossible to read.
8.holds: At the well that folds faces, the Genie priced the locals' wishes and found Boof's small asks would not come out to a number.

wonder.says: The same room's prices, quoted by the ones who finish the job themselves.

9.reason: A missing thing needs an outline before it can be missed. Eight honks laid on a ridge give the reader a hole the exact size of what they have been carrying.
9.holds: Eight honks lay on the ridge as shards, and put together they left one hole, exactly egg-sized.

ways: A ninth can still be made

10.reason: Could and cost have both had their say. Bone.land asks only what remains, and the hall is honest so there is one room in the book that will not flatter anybody.
10.holds: In Bone.land the great frame bore the egg, and the answer rang through every beam: the smallest wishes have the longest arcs. Mr. BaneWAP stopped waiting.

wonder.says: A felt mallet asks. An iron one tells.
wonder.asks: Does a struck beam answer the same way?

11.reason: The reader has to see a grand wish granted in full, or wishing for less would look like a failure of nerve. So it arrives at once, and the book lets him have it.
11.holds: Mr. BaneWAP took the egg and wished an empire. It came at once, hollow as a rented crown. His hoarded berries woke inside him, and the egg rolled back warm to Boof.

wonder.says: The bloom only might. Nothing has been granted yet.
wonder.asks: If it had only been a might, what would he have done?

12.reason: A confluence is the book's idea of an ending: everyone arrives, nothing is flattened, and the receipts hang side by side. Boof's wish is small on purpose. It has to fit in a mouth.
12.holds: At the meeting of two rivers Boof named her wish, one warm furrow kept open for whatever arrives next without a receipt. The Genie priced it honestly and walked upstream to become an echo.

wonder.says: The same crossing, from the person who has never bailed one water with the other's can.
wonder.asks: What does the ferryman think he saw?
ways: Forty years of the same thing

13.reason: The book closes everything except one brace, on purpose, because a serial needs a door and a reader needs somewhere to stand afterwards.
13.holds: The spent wish sounded as the ninth honk, the maps took the ink at last, and the last line was left blank.

wonder.says: A might becomes a ground: the unwritten line is somewhere to stand.
wonder.asks: Who fills in the last line?

14.reason: Book Two starts by collecting a debt the first book ran up. A day goes missing so the reader can see who keeps time for its own sake, and the field and the dog keep it without being asked.
14.holds: The Genie's price came due and a Thursday went missing from everyone's week but not from the field. On the day nobody kept, Boof found someone standing under a hat.

wonder.says: The berries' quarter turn, read from the hat.
ways: They were never facing the same way

15.reason: A record can be accurate and still miss what came through. Three careful hands write down one stranger three ways, so the reader has to hold all three and leave a box open.
15.holds: A porter held the parcel gate through a storm for a stranger, and by morning three honest records disagreed about what came through.

wonder.says: The same three records, from the one who held the gate.

pairs.name: The two pies, in separate rooms
pairs.primes: Mr. BoonWAP and Mr. BaneWAP are never in the same room. One passage is told another way, and marked where it changes.
pairs.why: Their one shared room is the bridge in Chapter Twelve, where a bitter pie is received warm. It is the book's idea of forgiveness, and some readers would rather not be asked to watch it.
pairs.costs: You keep the apology and lose the welcome. In the lanes their themes no longer answer each other in Six, Ten and Twelve.

swaps.para: And Mr. BoonWAP — who serves himself
swaps.text: Nobody came up the road to receive them. Mr. BoonWAP was in Bonk City that day, at his own table, where he had set out a plate and where, in this copy of the book, he is going to stay. The slices lay on the planks in the cold, exactly as large as they had been cut, and Mr. BaneWAP stood beside them a good deal smaller, finding out that giving is subtraction when nobody takes it.

The ferryman looked the slices over and left them where they lay, since they were not his to take. Mr. BaneWAP opened his mouth to announce something dreadful, from habit, and found he had nothing dreadful left. He announced instead that he would be very bitter about all of this, starting tomorrow, unless somebody was kind to him first. The ferryman knocked his pipe out on the rail, filled it again, and held it out to him stem first. It was the first thing Mr. BaneWAP had ever foretold that came true the kind way, and neither of them remarked on it. Boof smelled it go by: plum-dark at the bottom still, and sweet all the way up.

swaps.to: one slice left on the road for whoever comes

pairs.name: Boof and Mr. BaneWAP, never in a room
pairs.primes: Two chapters step out and are told in a line each, and one passage is told another way.
pairs.why: He argues against her at the council and takes the egg from her sling by hand. A household may want the dog and the announcer kept apart, and the book can bear it, since the rest of what he does reaches her by envelope, by rumour, or down a road.
pairs.costs: You give up the council and the seizure, which are where the book argues with itself. A line at the next chapter says what each held.

swaps.find: all the way out to where Boof stood
swaps.to: out to the middle of the span, while Boof stayed at the far end with her back to the rail

pairs.name: Clowns and mimes, on different days
pairs.primes: The lanes send no mimes. The pie words stay as they are, and nobody contests a chapter.
pairs.why: They are the lanes' own quarrel and never share a room in the book. Some people like one and not the other, and some would rather not have either coming at them with feeling.
pairs.costs: No march, no walls, nobody to out-do. A chapter the mimes already hold can still be won back with clowns.

held.why: She works for the land and they keep it warm. A chapter without them would be set somewhere else.
His price is the plot of both books. Set Chapter Three aside if you like, and the Thursday will still come due.
Book Two's question is what she notices before anyone has a word for it. Set Fourteen or Fifteen aside if you would rather not meet them yet.
The gate held for a stranger is the chapter. Without the stranger he is a man lifting a gate.
